newsitem.title: UK: U.S. weather supports oil but losses beckon.
newsitem.headline: U.S. weather supports oil but losses beckon.

text.p: Oil's headlong rush lower paused on Thursday as weekend weather forecasts pointed to higher heating fuel demand in the United States but analysts said the respite would be short-lived.
World benchmark Brent crude futures for June delivery gained ten cents to $17.91 a barrel by 1606 GMT on London's International Petroleum Exchange, bouncing off a session low of $17.66.

Dealers said forecasts of below normal temperatures until at least Saturday in the U.S. Northeast, the world's biggest heating oil market, helped steady nerves after recent losses prompted by rising U.S. stocks and a slow start to the spring gasoline season.

But high industry stocks -- the legacy of a relatively mild northern hemisphere winter -- combined with robust supply growth from the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and elsewhere would soon force prices lower again.
"Today's rally is just a pit stop on the race down," said Peter Gignoux, head of the energy desk at brokers Smith, Barney in London.

And even a slowdown in global tanker sailings, suggesting suppliers may be adjusting to lower second quarter demand, may be too little too late to prevent oil markets heading further back towards nine-month lows seen last week.
"The carry over from the winter will continue to impact on the system for a while yet," said Roy Mason of industry consultants Oil Movements.
"Offshore oil accumulated early in the year is swelling onshore stocks and will go on doing that for a while yet. The cavalry is on the way, but the fort may not last," he said in a weekly report.

After shedding $7 a barrel, or nearly 30 percent since the start of the year, oil prices have been treading water recently in anticipation of a surge in U.S. gasoline demand to fuel the summer driving season.
But the country's leading oil industry association said on Wednesday domestic gasoline supplies are expected to be more than sufficient to satisfy even the most bullish forecasts for demand growth.
In its annual outlook for the summer, the American Petroleum Institute (API) said gasoline supply would meet demand, even if it grew by 2.5 percent.
Earlier this month, the U.S. Department of Energy said it expected gasoline demand to grow by 1.8 percent this month.
But U.S. heating oil prices provided a degree of relief on Thursday as an early spring cold spell in the U.S. Northeast left one major supplier, Sun Co Inc, out of product until late next week.
Private forecaster Weather Services Corp (WSC) said temperatures would run two to six degrees Fahrenheit below normal on Thursday, dipping to between six and 12 degrees below normal on Saturday.
"There is the possibility of some snow developing in the higher elevations on Friday," WSC said.
